review:
Ah, Braveland. It's hard to know what to say about it. It is not a bad game. I'm tempted to call it good. But I'm not going to do that, and I wouldn't recommend it to people.

At $4.99, Braveland seems reasonably priced. On sale, it might even sound like a steal. But you're going to get a few hours out of it, and there's nothing remarkable about those few hours.

There's nothing really awful about Braveland. The graphics are slightly unnervingly Fisher Price, but they're effective and the backgrounds look nice. There are only a few songs, and they sound competent and appropriate. The interface is fine. The mechanics are... well, balanced and kind of standard for this kind of game.

So what's the problem?

There's not much depth to the battles, and there's not much to it besides battles. You pick up a modest variety of classes, and can bring up to five with you: archers, healers, knights, scouts, etc. Their roles are fairly obvious and they do them well enough. But you can really use whatever combination you want, and the gameplay won't change much at all.

The story is... well, the dialog is spelled and formatted correctly and does tell a pretty straightforward story about soldiers, bandits, villagers and the like. No one really says anything very interesting, but the conversations are short and inoffensive. The most personality you get out of the game is that bandits are dime-a-dozen jerks, and your peasant friend is a bit of a coward. There's a hero, who doesn't actually fight, and annoys me a little to look at him strutting around the world map as though he's helping. Technically he provides stat bonuses to the rest of the team by leveling up, but he mostly just speaks for the team and collects power-ups.

There's no real replay value to the campaign, but there's a Survival mode where you can play battle to battle, losing characters and buying new ones, and see how far you get. I played around with it a little, and it might add a bit of life to the game if you wind up loving it. So, there's a bit of hope for getting more play out of the game at least.

I have played a lot of Flash games in my days, on sites like Newgrounds - RPGs, tower defense, strategy games, action, etc.. Braveland feels very much like one of those games. The look, the feel, the length, the design choices and the options the player is given. Indeed, I feel like I've played Bravelands many times already. Except usually, when I play this kind of game, it's free. Often, it's also got something more novel or fun about it.

Normally, it's probably not good to get lost in the weeds talking about free vs. paid gaming in a review like this. I guess all I'm saying is, Bravelands is a dime a dozen kind of game that you see all over the internet, and even if it's got a bit of polish and isn't awful, it's hard for me to justify anyone spending their money on it. For a few dollars more, there are lots of really unique, memorable games on Steam.

You also acquire coins to spend on units, unit special abilities as well as four things for your hero to wear/weapon. You will also have a special ability to use during battle, as if your hero calls when to use it.  There will be 5 abilities total as you advance on the map and unlock them.

The game breaks down to being able to buy enough units and knowing which ones to use and not waste coins spending them on units you will not be using later and how you move your units on the battlefield. Battles are turn-based with very few options to use for your units. You can move, delay your move, attack or put up a defense each turn for your units. Nearly all units have a special ability that you can choose to use, however once used you will have to wait a few turns before you can use it again.

Game is recommended as a first RPG game to get the feel of it, if the player is playing for the first time. If you want a challenge, avoid. Best to get on sale as well, as there isn't a lot of playtime involved, I have 23.4 hours in the game but left it running a few times while doing chores. Hear ye, hear ye. Your land is in turmoil. Bandits rampaged your town and currently going on a raiding frenzy. You, a rag tag farmer decided to rise up to do away those bandits. So, your quest begins by searching the lands (in linear fashion), recruit your army and fight your adversaries in hexagonal combat battlefields all displayed in hand drawn yet beautiful art. So, what are you waiting for? Oh, this sounds familiar, way too familiar to your liking? You guessed right. Braveland, even though it looks gorgeous, doesn’t bring anything new to the turned based hexagonal combat system. Heck, even the plot is ho-hum to the max as the entire game is simply fighting one mob to the next until the game ends.

It may sound I’m a little too harsh with this and yes, I am. There’s nothing really going for in this game other than the artwork. The game is a mobile phone port and that, in itself, is not too bad considering I have played ported mobile games that actually fared well (e.g. Galaxy on Fire 2 Full HD). What made it sub-standard is there’s very little that caught my attention wanting to see what’s next in store. It’s all a matter of fighting one battle to the next until the game ends. At least add an interesting plotline however that was not the case too. So, all you have left is the visuals and sounds. The visuals I have to admit are pretty to look at – all sugary with a cherry on top that doesn’t overstay its usefulness and the musical scores are brilliantly composed and well suited for this style of game.

How the game plays out, you have a world map to explore aiming to recruit your armies to finish off those malicious bandits that destroyed your town. You cannot get lost in the world as the available path is drawn out for you so it’s a matter of following the leader (so to speak). During your adventures, you’ll get the opportunity to hire men-at-arms and even ‘stray’ off the beaten track to gain further enhancements for your army. But of course, everything will result in combat, not matter what. The only exception is when you locate a store to buy equipment and / or more cannon fodder. But to get to those places is guarded by mobs so you can say every damn movement equals to combat.

How the combat plays out is displayed in a battlefield of sorts. Drawn in hexagonal shapes so your movement is governed by six directions. Your army stands on the left and right, the enemies. Both armies can be a mixture of critters, archers, warriors, golems and so on. However, the important factor is the number of solders stacked in that group. Basically, the higher the number, the deadlier they become. In a nutshell, it plays upon strength in numbers.
Also, each combatant is governed by statistics to measure their qualities so this is where the minimal RPG elements comes in. The statistics ranges from armour to damage output to speed and so on. Granted the game does extremely well with its tooltips as you can view their stats anytime without too many clicks - simple yet effective. Also, each troop have a special ability to spice things up yet they require a cool down once activated. I actually smiled at one of the enemy’s special ability where the archer’s special ability is they occasionally miss. I wish there’s more silliness like this however it wasn’t the case.

Another skill that’s capable to turn the tides of battle is the rage meter. What this does that every time your character gets hit, builds up rage. And once you accumulate a certain number of rage points can launch a rage spell like fire arrow or boost armour (to name a few). Take note that rage skills can only be found and not earned however they are worthwhile investments as it does not take up a movement point and heck, it’s a bonus as it’s governed by the number of hits your group takes.

As far as tactics is concerned, the battlefield does have some ‘roadblocks’ that can assist you ‘bottlenecking’ the enemy (and vice versa). However, that tactic for me had marginal success as there’s normally a mob group that moves around this roadblock and attack your weak armoured soldiers, namely the archers / healers. There’s nothing wrong with that and I applaud this tactic. However, because I played the game on hard difficulty, I cannot say whether these happens at the lower difficulty levels.

So, what I normally do before combat starts is to see if I can create a roadblock. After that, I analyse which enemy’s secondary skill will cause me grief and then once spotted, gang bang this group with all my troops. Next to see which group has a high soldier count as the game does plays upon strength in numbers. Dwindle their numbers down by using your archers / healers. Then mop up the rest. This thought pattern has won me a lot of battles and granted, there are some battles that comes down to just two, my warriors vs enemy archers, for instance. That was pretty cool as it went down to the wire.

There were times that the landscape displayed groups of tough enemies as my next encounter that I need to defeat them however just couldn’t. Caused me a little concern as it could spell game over just because I couldn’t defeat any of them. Yeah, I can knock down the difficulty level however in doing so ruin a certain achievement. However, luck played its role and looking in hindsight, was also pretty cool. So, the troop balancing is pretty spot on in most parts – well I guess for my playing style at least. My style mainly consists of having heavily armoured soldiers and a good set of archers in the back as I found that the healers are a joke. Weak armoured, weak attacking spells and only have two healing spells per battle is a waste of troop space for me.

To complete the game can take approximately five hours or so. For me on hard, it took me about six hours to complete. Also, because there’s no grinding to level up and earning extra gold, every combat counts. Because of this makes you think twice spending gold as there’s no way you will be swimming in it. That’s another bonus to this game however take note I’m basing this on hard so it could be different playing on the lower difficulty level.

To those achievement hunters, there are twenty-one to accumulate and I managed to snag sixteen during my first run. Looking back on them now, you can snag all of them in a single playthrough as well. Also, because the game is linear, there’s no real reason to play it again. That’s fine in my eyes if the main campaign had a decent length and interesting (and not just having one hundred go fetch quests). I guess gameplay length is the bane of most mobile gaming in general so it would be nicer if the PC port has extra missions. But that requires more effort on the developer’s behalf and we all don’t want that to happen aye. In additional to this, there are five steam cards to collect and even though the cards are pictures from the game, they all quite nice to use as background wallpapers. Heck I using one right now.

So, with all this negativity and a handful of positives as explained above, it would be hard pressed to recommend this game to anyone other than those who likes a quick bash waiting for the train to arrive (so to speak) or even want a taste for this style of ‘war gaming’ experience. Even the price tag of approximately USD $5 may be tempting (subject to exchange rates if you are not in the US) however I still believe there are better games out there even if your goal is to kill a bit of time.

You liked Heroes of Might & Magic? Or perhaps King's Bounty or Age of Wonders? Stripped of all city management, you basically just have the turn-based combat. Braveland takes this and adds a big, friendly smile on every creature.

It presents you a cute, classic storyline: a happy farmer boy loses his family and farm to bandits and sets out on a bold journey for revenge, but it turns out there is something more sinister going on and the happy guy wants to deal with it. He travels around and beats up the bad guys who take the hits with permanent crooked smiles on their faces. At first the dialogue attemps some meme-based humour (arrow in the knee anyone?), but they are quickly discarded for cheerful, repetitive greetings and taunts.

Travelling happens on a board with enemies, stores and events in each tile. It's linear, though you can (and should) check every branching road for bonus items, gold and experience points. Gold gets you more troops and items, experience gives small bonuses to creature stats and increases the cap on troops.

While I only played the hard mode, combats are easy for a player familiar with turn-based strategy games. Combat AI does not offer surprises in neither good nor bad ways, so it's okay. There are only 7 different types of troops to buy and around the same number of different enemies with upgraded versions of the usual ones coming later into the game. Basically all of them also smile all the time.

Why, I even lost one battle! Being vastly out-numbered, my troops collected their pocket money and gave it to me to hire more troops for another try. Happyland would have been a more appropriate name for the game.

In conclusion, Braveland would probably be a nice introduction to turn-based strategy games for children or people not acquainted with the genre. For the rest of us it's just a small snack (it lasted ~4 hours for me) that gets a dusty taste towards the end. Get it on sale.

Oh yeah, and find or buy a little loot along the way.

As a fan of Tactical RPGs, I saw that Braveland was on a sale and decided to pick it up and give it a shot. Although it seemingly does all that the developers intended, I was not impressed and quickly became bored of it. Some may enjoy it, particularly if they are into simpler strategy games, but the extremely casual nature of the game left me continually wishing there was more to it.

The story of the game is about as generic as they come; a simple country boy who's village was destroyed becomes a hero. The mechanics aren't much better than that. You and your army level up and improve with both experience and equipment but there's very little in the way of customizing your forces that most games in this genre have at this point. The combat itself is mediocre, feeling like a simplified version of the older entries in the Heroes of Might & Magic series.

Not a bad game, just one that failed to pique my interest, much less hold it. I would recommend it to those looking for a very casual Tactical RPG game that doesn't offer much but can pass a few minutes here and there. I would absolutely not recommend it to anyone looking for something deeper than that. Braveland does exactly what it says, nothing more, nothing less, and fails to bring any innovation to the genre.

Braveland is a super addictive strategy RPG with simplified mechanics and scope. You level up, improve  stats, equip items, maintain your army and teach each unit type one special skill. But you only pick one stat out of 2 every time you level up, you have less than 5 items per category to equip for your hero and there are 7 different units. I’m not implying it’s a bad thing as it works perfectly for a game that’s around 6 hours long (on hard). The story is also very one note and super basic, the dialogues can be funny though. It’s a game that’s very easy to get into, the style is pretty cute and it’s an enjoyable experience.

I mostly have 2 issues with the game. The achievements are mostly fair and fun, one requires you to complete the game on hard which is a fine idea. But, there is absolutely a wrong way of spending money to keep up with the challenge. At first I thought it would be better to prioritise items as their stats affect all units. This made the game a chore with constant deaths, it was clear that I was doing something wrong. It turns out that it’s a must to invest most of the money into increasing the number of fighters within a unit. This forced me to quit my save about one third of the game and start a new save since you can’t grind, there are no replacements for the enemies you defeat. It made such a world of difference that I’m worried this could drastically change someone’s impression/experience if they don’t know. Also, text is often outside the text box on a 2560 x 1440p monitor.

Braveland is not necessarily special and it doesn’t do anything differently. But it’s a fine game that’s well put together and it doesn’t ask a high price. €10 based on what I experienced is fair but you don’t even need to pay that. It’s still on sale for €1 on steam at the moment. If you’re looking for a short and casual strategy RPG, then this fits the bill. I’ve spent 7.8 hours on the game with all the achievements, but that does include my first incomplete save which I estimate to have taken me 2 hours before I quit.

[h1]Shallow and repetitive[/h1]

Braveland is a tactical RPG developed by Tortuga Games and published by PlayPanic. It was made as a primarily mobile game and then was ported to PC.

I've bought this game because I'm a huge fan of the King's Bounty series and this one is an obvious King's Bounty clone. However it pales in comparison to King's Bounty by any possible metric, and being mobile-first is not a legit excuse for that.

[h2]Gameplay or lack thereof[/h2]
Braveland has two interconnecting modes: adventure and battle. During adventuring, the player follows a highly linear story path, progressing by traveling between pre-defined nodes. A single node can contain either a treasure, a shop, enemy troops or an altar. The main problem appears from the very start: [i]the variability or freedom is near-non-existing.[/i] There's some semblance of non-linearity in the form of off-path nodes but it becomes pretty obvious that those nodes are either:
[list]
    [*]Obligatory, since without them it'd be, depending on the difficulty, either impossible or extremely tedious to progress
    [*]Useless as they do not provide anything of importance except a few dialogue prompts.
[/list]
That's it. There's nothing in between. You don't really have any optional quests or encounters you can skip or ignore. You can keep an enemy encounter for later ([i] which is the optimal strategy[/i]) but apart from that there're no other real choices you can make. 

To top it off, the game suffers from the highly tedious backtracking implementation. When you want to buy out more units, you would have to go to one of the shops, and shops usually contain 1 or 2 of the specific units, which can also run out. In the "late" game you're forced to get through the whole map to refresh your army which can take a few minutes, and then you also have to get back...

[h2]Fighting the foes[/h2]
When the player attacks enemy troops, a battle starts. It is a typical for the genre, hex-based turn-based battle arena, known to anyone who's ever played any games from King's Bounty or HoMM series. 

What is new thing though, is almost  complete lack of player agency, which is again a symptom of insufficient polishing. For example, it is impossible to change the position of your unit stack in the army or to split said stack which is [b]highly important[/b] for this genre,

Among other issues there are:
[list]
    [*]The tutorial guide shows up in the battle even if you disable it.
    [*]You can't do any action, including closing the game/reloading the save file until all enemy stacks have acted. But at least there's an option to speed up combat animations.
    [*]The unit inspection window works very strangely. Sometimes you just can't find the hitbox and have to click 2 or 3 times in a row, which is pretty annoying.
[/list]

You can check the upcoming turns' sequence and unit's current health bar, which is an unexpectedly good feature for a game of [i]this[/i] quality to have. The post-battle screen is also fine and pretty informative.

The unit variety is OK for the game of this scope and there're some special keywords and abilities [i]that could have created enough variety[/i], if it wasn't for other, numerous problems. For example, you can't hire any enemy units, which just doesn't make sense. That limits the player to picking from the roster of seven units in total, which is too small an amount to allow for any unique strategies

The decision to let the player unlock your units' abilities (for money) is interesting in theory, but the way it's done it feels clunky as well. First of all, you have to do that for almost any hireable unit, which feels lame; then, for most of the time, you get an upgrade almost immediately after getting the unit you can upgrade, which is also lame. And finally, there's no variety in that either since you do not really have any choice between different abilities or whom to upgrade first since any unit can have only a single ability and the gold is always in abudance.

There's also some "bosses" but they are bosses only in name since it's just recolored enemy units you have already met by that time.

[h2]Progression[/h2]
Now this is the main culprit why I left a negative review. Not overflowing, barely readable text prompts, nor the linear "main quest" or some debatable game-design decisions, but this. 

Everything mentioned above is layered upon innate and extreme lack of an interesting progression system. The game's progression system works like that: you fight enemies, you get experience, level up, have a leadership upgrade and choose one of two random attribute bonuses. 

Attribute system is mostly fine, you have four attributes: [b]Attack[/b], [b]Endurance[/b], [b]Spirit[/b] and [b]Knowledge[/b]. Endurance and Knowledge increase physical/magical damage resistance of your units (but nowhere does it say by how much) while Attack increases their output damage (once again, God knows by how much). The Spirit increase your maximum and starting Rage (game's Mana analogue, which it humbly appropriated from King's Bounty) and damage output from spells.

The main problem is with Leadership, or, to be specific, the system around it. Just like in King's Bounty, the player's army size is limited by their Leadership. The thing is, any unit has a star rating (I'm gonna call it [i]level[/i] for simplicity) and it too defines what kind of units you can have in your army. You have up to 15 levels in your whole army in total, meaning you just can't have a half of possible unit combinations that are [b]already limitied by small unit roster, leadership and gold expenses[/b].

It deprives the game of any left non-linearity, basically shoehorning it into the very same playstyle, unit roster and upgrade choices every time, leaving zero room for non-torturous replayability. That, coupled with fact that game is itself very short, give a superficial, content-less impression. (I've been trying to have a no-loss run on Hard, replaying almost every single battle few times and it took me 60-70 mintues to get through the campaign).

As if it wasn't bland enough, there's no high stakes or any challenge at all. If you lose your units they get resurrected for a very small amount of gold. Strangely enough, this allows you to softlock yourself by spending too much gold before fighting a strong enemy. After that you don't have the gold to buy new units and can't continue playing since your army's too weak to progress.

Items also suck - the following item is almost either better than previous one or useless and there's only 3 or 4 different items for every slot, so once again, the same thing: lack of variability under the thin veil of pretend non-linearity.


[h2]Few good things[/h2]
If you have read up this review to this point you may think that this game is completely bad, which is not true. I really tried to like the game, and there are some redeeming qualities. First of all, graphics and stylization is pretty good, music is basic but it works properly - by creating a fitting low-fantasy vibe.

Core gameplay of battle mode is also solid - there are classical wait/defense up options; there are some chests scattered around the battlefield that you can pick up for additional gold; attribute-upgrading altars are fun and physical/magical unit division does work properly.

This game has potential, but the devs have chosen linear and safe approach that doesn't demand much resources and time. That's a shame cause there's huge market gap for the games of this sort.

You essentially buy units, a few items to boost your 4 stats, and a few special attacks.

The game has no real replay value once you beat it and have all the achievements, if that is your thing. There is a Survival mini-game that unlocks, but it is just a beat 10 battle grids sort of thing without being defeated and you have at least one unit that isn't available in the regular game. However, in the Survival game, if you lose units, they are gone.

There is no grinding with the exception of if you lose a battle. Then you essentially restart in the spot just before the battle without really losing anything. You even make a little money. At the end of each battle, you get a monetary reward, minus the cost of replacing your units. So even if an entire unit is killed, you don't lose them or have to go back and buy them over again.

Your Hero doesn't appear on the battlefield, doesn't participate, and there isn't any character customization. The units are tiered in value and the most you can ever have is 15 total score in units. The units are valued from 1-5. Once you get the hang of combat, know the enemy strengths and weaknesses, and those of the units, the game isn't really that hard, even on Hard.

Braveland is very much a KINDA game. It plays KINDA like King's Bounty, only much more shallow. The music is KINDA "Sir John Backsword", although not really. It's all very mobile, very casual (if you lose a fight, nothing happens—you even get rewarded!), and very unoriginal.

However, what the game lacks in originality, it makes up for in charm. I enjoyed the units' descriptions and overall tone. Still, it doesn't really belong on PC—there's just too little to be done in the game; it's a "play while you commute" kind of thing. I suggest you buy it on mobile.

Braveland offers grid combat inspired by classics like Heroes of Might & Magic and King’s Bounty, making battles strategic yet easy to grasp.

You begin as a young farmer seeking justice, gradually building an army of peasants, archers, and knights while unlocking new abilities.
The progression feels rewarding, with each victory giving you gold, fame, and stronger troops.
It’s easy to learn, visually appealing, and steadily rewarding.

This is my review for Braveland ; (6.5/10)

Storyline: The storyline is dull and unintresting (atleast for me) it's one of those turn-based basic games, where it's focused on the combat and character elements rather than on the levels of story.
You get to move along the map while meeting friendlies/enemies and having this typicall "chat bubbles". I just skip those lol. (2/10)

Gameplay: Unlike the aspect of the story, the gameplay itself is enjoyable for a turn-based strategy game.  (8/10)

1- Character Elements -
@You can view each character's information which include: health, damage, defence , range of movement and number of turns. There is also a description of character abilities and what it's capable of (stunning/magic damage/healing etc)
@Level System: You level up by getting exp (obviously) by defeating and winning enemies. 
@Main Character: You buy more units or upgrades with the coins you get, you can't upgrade your units and however, you cannot fight with your main character (you only fight with your 'squad' aka your units)

2- Combat- 
The combat is fun and easy. You get tips in the start of the game to understand the basics, and then you will just get used to the combat and know what to do.
There are some points however, where you will have to move forward and fight weaker enemies instead of trying to beat an overwhelming enemy squad because your squad is not strong enough (which makes the game challenging.)

Gameplay Styles: (5/10)
3 Difficulties (Set to Easy/Normal/Hard)
Easy is too easy , Normal is challenging enough and Hard oh well, it's for those of you who want to hit your head in the computer in order to win each match even if you have for example 5 units and your enemies have 500.

Enjoyment: the game is fun for a regular and basic turn based game, I recommend it (it's not have so many
hours of gameplay either so it's just for fun for your free time) - (4/5)

Repeatable: Didn't finish the game yet, but it's one of those turn-based games which the difficulty is the only thing that will change your gameplay. (1.5/5)

Frustration: Except for extremely unexpected challenging enemies (bosses with 300 health and 2 units of it) the game is fluent and you will feel like a god playing with your super talented squad. - (2/5)

Boredom: You will play this game for few hours without breaks. (1/5)

Fun small casual game with easy mechanics, good tutorial and a linear story. It's a charming mini version of Heroes of Might & Magic just without the building (town development) aspect. Around 10 enemy types and allies, most with a special skill to be unlocked (purchased) as you play. A huge plus is that after each fight you don't have to restock on soldiers but rather you have automatically gold deducted from the reward to "revive" your wounded army. Instead, you purchase soldiers as your hero levels up and you gain more slots. I wish there was more weapons/armor available, but other than that skill variation and stat variation is decent. Appropriate price tag.

Braveland is a simple mobile strategy game that was ported to PC. For the price, this game is a winner! Overall, the turn-based battles are the classic type of battles that games like “Heroes of Might & Magic” uses. It follows a linear campaign where the main character is a poor farmer who sets out to find the evil king and gets revenge for losing his village and family. 

In addition, to the campaign mode, Braveland also has a survivor mode. Survivor mode provides a more challenging battle environment than the campaign mode. Also, survivor mode places healing and combat limitations on certain units so the battles get tricky as additional thinking is required to survive to the next battle.

In conclusion, Braveland is nothing of a surprise, but it a good game to both beginners of turned-based strategy games and to veterans as well. Although it does lack replay value, the simple and easy gameplay is family friendly and it provides a few hours of quick enjoyable moments.
